strings.title: Adding Up to Subtract
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: When two numbers are close together, find the difference by counting up from the smaller number to the bigger one, using friendly landing spots.
strings.keywords: difference, count up, adding up, friendly number, distance between
watchFor: Counting back from the big number in ones: ask "How far apart are they? Could you start at the small number?"
Losing track of the jumps: ask "Which jumps are the answer? Add them up."
Regrouping errors with the algorithm on 403 − 397: ask "Are these numbers close together? How far is it from 397 to 400?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "When is counting up easier than taking away?" Land: when the numbers are close, the difference is the distance between them. Jump to a friendly number, then to the end, and add the jumps.

problems.notes: Look for: 38 up 2 to 40, up 10 to 50. Ask: "How far is it from 38 to 50?" Word choice: "difference", "distance". Model: numberline 38 >40 >50

responses.say: 38 up to 40 is 2, then 10 more to 50. 2 + 10 = 12.
responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: which numbers are the answer?

responses.say: Take away 30 is 20, take away 8 more is 12.
responses.tip: Taking away works too. Ask: which way had fewer steps?
Subtracted 0 − 8 as 8 − 0. Ask: is 38 + 28 = 50?

problems.notes: Look for: 64 up 6 to 70, up 30 to 100. Ask: "What's a friendly number to land on?" Model: numberline 64 >70 >100

responses.say: 64 up 6 is 70, then 30 more is 100. That's 36.
I went up 36 all at once because 64 + 36 = 100.
responses.tip: Knows the partner to 100. Ask: how did you know?
Common with partners of 100. Ask: is 64 + 46 = 100? Check the tens.

problems.notes: Look for: 285 up 5 to 290, up 10 to 300 (or 15 to 300). Ask: "Do you need to take away 285?" Model: numberline 285 >290 >300

responses.tip: Ask: what is 285 + 25? Is that 300?

problems.notes: Look for: 975 up 25 to 1000. Ask: "How is this like 100 − 75?" Model: numberline 975 >1000

responses.tip: Ask: how is this like 100 − 75?
Same difference. Ask: why did that work?
Ask: count up from 975. Where does 35 land?

problems.notes: Look for: 397 up 3 to 400, up 3 to 403. Ask: "Why is the algorithm hard here, and counting up easy?" Model: numberline 397 >400 >403

responses.tip: Algorithm slip with the zero. Ask: are 403 and 397 close or far apart?

problems.notes: Look for: 1989 up 11 to 2000, up 5 to 2005. Ask: "How many years between 1989 and 2005?" Model: numberline 1989 >1990 >2000 >2005

responses.say: 1989 to 1990 is 1, to 2000 is 10 more, then 5 more. 16.
responses.tip: A real use: how many years between two dates.
Ask: what is 1989 + 26? Is it 2005?

strings.title: Same Difference
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Add the same amount to both numbers and the difference stays the same. Slide the problem to one that subtracts a friendly number: 302 − 198 = 304 − 200.
strings.keywords: difference, same difference, slide, add to both, friendly number, distance
watchFor: Adding to one number and taking from the other (302 − 198 to 300 − 200): ask "Did the distance between them stay the same?"
Sliding the wrong number to a friendly one: ask "Which number would be easier to subtract?"
Regrouping across zeros in 1003 − 997: ask "Are these numbers close? Could you slide or count up?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why do we add the same amount to both?" Land: the difference is the distance between the numbers, and sliding both the same amount keeps the distance. Slide so you subtract a friendly number.

problems.notes: Look for: 53 − 20. Ask: "What could you add to both?" Word choice: "the difference stays the same". Model: slide 52 - 19 = 53 - 20

responses.tip: The target strategy.

responses.say: 19 up to 20 is 1, up to 52 is 32: 33.
responses.tip: Adding up. Also great.
Took 1 from 52 but added 1 to 19. Ask: are they still the same distance apart?

problems.notes: Look for: 304 − 200. Ask: "What does 198 need to be friendly?" Model: slide 302 - 198 = 304 - 200

responses.tip: Moved the numbers in opposite directions. Ask: did the distance change?

problems.notes: Look for: 503 − 300. Ask: "Which number should be friendly?" Model: slide 500 - 297 = 503 - 300

responses.tip: Took away 300, then took 3 more. Ask: is 300 more or less than 297? Should you give 3 back?

problems.notes: Look for: 1006 − 1000, or count up 3 and 3. Ask: "How far apart are they?" Model: slide 1003 - 997 = 1006 - 1000

responses.tip: Counting up. Best when numbers are close.
Regrouping slip. Ask: count up from 997. Where do you land?

problems.notes: Look for: 4002 − 2000. Ask: "How does the slide help with all those zeros?" Model: slide 4000 - 1998 = 4002 - 2000

responses.tip: No regrouping needed.
Rounded and forgot to adjust. Ask: 1998 is less than 2000, so is the answer more or less than 2000?

problems.notes: Look for: 7007 − 4000. Ask: "How much do you add to both?" Model: slide 7002 - 3995 = 7007 - 4000

strings.title: Back to a Ten
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Take away in friendly jumps: the tens first, then back to a ten, then the rest. 53 − 27 is 53 − 20 − 3 − 4.
strings.keywords: take away, jump back, tens first, back to a ten, number line
watchFor: Subtracting the smaller digit from the bigger one (53 − 27 = 34): ask "Can you take 7 from 3? What could you do instead?"
Jumping back one at a time: ask "Could you take the tens away in one jump?"
Losing track of how much has been taken away: ask "How much have you taken so far? How much is left to take?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why did we stop at 30 on the way down?" Land: take the tens in one jump, then jump back to a ten, then take the rest. Splitting the number you take away makes each jump friendly.

problems.notes: Look for: 5 tens take away 2 tens. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 50 -20

responses.say: 5 tens take away 2 tens is 3 tens.

problems.notes: Look for: the 3 ones just come along. Ask: "What changed from the last one?" Model: numberline 53 -20
Look for: back 20, then back 3 to land on 30. Ask: "Why is it a friendly answer?" Model: numberline 53 -20 -3

responses.tip: Landing on a ten.

problems.notes: Look for: back 20, back 3 to 30, back 4 more. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Word choice: "jump back to a ten". Model: numberline 53 -20 -3 -4

responses.say: Back 20 to 33, back 3 to 30, back 4 to 26.
responses.tip: The target strategy.

responses.say: 27 up to 30 is 3, then up to 53 is 23: 26.
responses.tip: Adding up. Also great.
Took 3 from 7 in the ones. Ask: can you take 7 from 3? Check: is 27 + 34 = 53?

problems.notes: Look for: back 30 to 52, back 2 to 50, back 3 to 47. Ask: "Where's the friendly ten this time?" Model: numberline 82 -30 -2 -3

responses.tip: Bigger digit minus smaller in the ones. Ask: is 35 + 53 = 82?

problems.notes: Look for: back 30 to 34, back 4 to 30, back 4 more. Ask: "How did you split the 8?" Model: numberline 64 -30 -4 -4

responses.say: Back 30 to 34, back 4 to 30, back 4 to 26.

responses.tip: Take too much, then add back.

problems.notes: Look for: back 40 to 85, back 5 to 80, back 2 to 78. Ask: "Does it still work past 100?" Model: numberline 125 -40 -5 -2

strings.title: Up to a Hundred
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: To subtract from 100, 200 or 1000, count up from the smaller number to the next ten, then to the hundred.
strings.keywords: count up, partners of 100, next ten, distance, difference
watchFor: Making 10 in each column (100 − 73 = 37): ask "Does 73 + 37 make 100?"
Forgetting the jump to the next ten: ask "How far is 73 from 80? From 80 to 100?"
Treating 200 − 148 like 100 − 48 and stopping: ask "How far is 148 from 200?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is counting up easier than taking away here?" Land: from 73, jump to the next ten (80), then to 100, and add the jumps. Check by adding back.

problems.notes: Look for: 70 + 30 = 100. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 70 >100
Look for: 73 up 7 to 80, up 20 to 100. Ask: "What's the next ten after 73?" Word choice: "count up". Model: numberline 73 >80 >100

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Made 10 in each column. Ask: is 73 + 37 = 100?

problems.notes: Look for: 2 to 50, 50 more to 100. Ask: "Which jump was easiest?" Model: numberline 48 >50 >100

responses.tip: Ask: count up from 48. Where does 62 land?

problems.notes: Look for: the same jumps as the last one. Ask: "What do you notice?" Model: numberline 148 >150 >200

responses.tip: Ask: why is it the same answer?

problems.notes: Look for: 4 to 230, 70 to 300. Ask: "What's the next ten?" Model: numberline 226 >230 >300

responses.tip: Ask: about how far is 226 from 300? Is 126 sensible?

problems.notes: Look for: 50 to 700, 300 to 1000. Ask: "Is it the same idea with a thousand?" Model: numberline 650 >700 >1000
Look for: 75 to 700, 300 to 1000. Ask: "What does 625 need to make 700?" Model: numberline 625 >700 >1000

strings.title: Take Too Much, Then Add Back
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: When the number you take away is close to a ten or a hundred, take away the friendly number, then add back the extra: 75 − 29 is 75 − 30 + 1.
strings.keywords: take away a friendly number, add back, too much, compensate
watchFor: Taking away the extra too (60 − 9 = 60 − 10 − 1 = 49): ask "Did you take away too much or too little? Which way do you fix it?"
Adding back the wrong amount: ask "How much more is 30 than 29?"
Doing it digit by digit: ask "Is 29 close to a friendly number?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why do we add back after taking too much?" Land: we took away more than we needed, so we give the extra back. 75 − 29 = 75 − 30 + 1.

problems.notes: Look for: a quick ten. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 60 -10
Look for: take 10, give 1 back. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Word choice: "took away too much". Model: numberline 60 -10 +1

responses.say: 60 − 10 is 50, but I only needed to take 9, so add 1 back: 51.
responses.tip: The target strategy.
Took the extra away too. Ask: did you take too much or too little?

problems.notes: Look for: take 20, give 1 back. Ask: "What's 19 close to?" Model: numberline 75 -20 +1
Look for: take 30, give 1 back. Ask: "What's the same as the last one?" Model: numberline 75 -30 +1

responses.say: Back 20 to 55, back 5 to 50, back 4 to 46.
responses.tip: Back to a ten. Also great.

problems.notes: Look for: take 50, give 2 back. Ask: "How much too much?" Model: numberline 132 -50 +2

responses.tip: Ask: did 50 take away too much or too little?

problems.notes: Look for: take 100, give 2 back. Ask: "Does it work with hundreds?" Model: numberline 250 -100 +2
Look for: take 200, give 1 back. Ask: "Which way is quicker than the algorithm?" Model: numberline 503 -200 +1

strings.title: Take Away or Add Up?
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Look at the numbers first. When you take away a small amount, take it away. When the two numbers are close together, count up the distance.
strings.keywords: take away, add up, distance, close together, choose a strategy
watchFor: Counting back 86 from 91: ask "Are 91 and 86 close together? Is there a quicker way?"
Counting up from 7 to 205: ask "Is 7 a small amount to take away?"
Using the same strategy for every problem: ask "What do you notice about these two numbers?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did you decide which way to go?" Land: small number to take away? Take it away. Numbers close together? Count up the distance. Both give the same answer, so pick the quicker one.

problems.notes: Look for: take 4 away, back 1 to 90, back 3. Ask: "Is 4 a lot to take away?" Model: numberline 91 -1 -3

responses.tip: Take away: small amount.

problems.notes: Look for: 86 up 4 to 90, up 1 to 91. Ask: "Why not take away 86?" Model: numberline 86 >90 >91

responses.tip: Add up: the numbers are close.
Ask: count up from 86. How many jumps to 91?

problems.notes: Look for: back 5 to 200, back 2. Ask: "Take away or add up?" Model: numberline 205 -5 -2

responses.tip: Ask: if you take 5 you're at 200. How much more to take?

problems.notes: Look for: 196 up 4 to 200, up 5 to 205. Ask: "What do you notice about these numbers?" Model: numberline 196 >200 >205

responses.tip: Algorithm slip. Ask: are 205 and 196 close together?

problems.notes: Look for: back 20, back 5. Ask: "Which way?" Model: numberline 340 -20 -5
Look for: 315 up 5 to 320, up 20 to 340. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline 315 >320 >340

responses.tip: The answer to the last one is the number here. Ask: why?

problems.notes: Look for: 994 up 6 to 1000, up 1. Ask: "Would you ever take away 994?" Model: numberline 994 >1000 >1001

strings.title: Subtracting Near a Thousand
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: When both numbers are near a hundred or a thousand, count up through the friendly numbers, or slide both numbers so you subtract a friendly one.
strings.keywords: count up, hundreds, thousands, same difference, friendly number, distance
watchFor: Regrouping across the zeros in 1002 − 898 and getting lost: ask "How far is 898 from 900?"
Counting up and forgetting a jump: ask "Which jumps make the answer? Add them all."
Sliding one number but not the other: ask "Did you add the same to both?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why are these easier than they look?" Land: the numbers are close to hundreds and thousands, so count up through them, or slide both so you subtract a friendly number.

problems.notes: Look for: 9 hundreds to 10 hundreds. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 900 >1000
Look for: 100 more, plus 2. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline 900 >1000 >1002
Look for: 898 up 2 to 900, then 102 more. Or slide: 1004 − 900. Ask: "What does 898 need?" Word choice: "count up through the hundred". Model: numberline 898 >900 >1000 >1002

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Same difference.
Regrouping slip with the zeros. Ask: are 1002 and 898 close together?

problems.notes: Look for: 4 to 1900, 100 to 2000, 4 more. Ask: "Is it the same idea?" Model: numberline 1896 >1900 >2000 >2004
Look for: 14 to 900, 100 to 1000, 5 more. Ask: "What's the first friendly number?" Model: numberline 886 >900 >1000 >1005

responses.tip: Ask: add the jumps again. 14 + 100 + 5?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 to 2900, 100 to 3000, 1 more. Ask: "Which strategy would you choose?" Model: numberline 2895 >2900 >3000 >3001
Look for: 3 to 4900, 100 to 5000, 3 more. Ask: "What do you notice about the last two?" Model: numberline 4897 >4900 >5000 >5003

strings.title: Zeros in the Way
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Subtracting from 400 or 1000 is tricky with the algorithm because of all the zeros. Count up instead, or slide both numbers down by 1 so there's nothing to regroup.
strings.keywords: zeros, count up, same difference, slide down 1, regroup
watchFor: Bottom minus top in each column (400 − 163 = 363): ask "Is 163 + 363 equal to 400?"
Regrouping across zeros and losing track: ask "Could you count up from 163 instead?"
Sliding only one number: ask "Did you take 1 from both?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did you get around the zeros?" Land: count up through friendly numbers (163 → 200 → 400), or take 1 from both numbers (399 − 162) so nothing needs regrouping.

problems.notes: Look for: 4 hundreds take 1 hundred. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 400 -100
Look for: 163 up 37 to 200, up 200 to 400. Or 399 − 162. Ask: "How could you avoid the zeros?" Word choice: "count up". Model: numberline 163 >170 >200 >400

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Same difference down 1.
Bottom minus top in each column. Ask: is 163 + 363 = 400?

problems.notes: Look for: 199 up 1 to 200, up 200 to 400. Ask: "What's 199 close to?" Model: numberline 199 >200 >400

responses.tip: Take too much, add back.

problems.notes: Look for: 245 up 5, up 50, up 300. Or 599 − 244. Ask: "Which way do you like?" Model: numberline 245 >250 >300 >600
Look for: 999 − 456, or count up 3, 40, 500. Ask: "Does sliding down 1 work for 1000 too?" Model: slide 1000 - 457 = 999 - 456
Look for: 1350 up 50 to 1400, up 600 to 2000. Ask: "What's the first friendly jump?" Model: numberline 1350 >1400 >2000
Look for: 2875 up 125 to 3000, up 2000. Ask: "What does 875 need to make 1000?" Model: numberline 2875 >2900 >3000 >5000
